newsitem.title: UK: Bank of England report to renew inflation warning.
newsitem.headline: Bank of England report to renew inflation warning.

text.p: The Bank of England is likely to renew its warnings about a pickup in inflation in the next two years and strongly urge a tightening in monetary policy when it publishes its quarterly Inflation Report on Wednesday.
The report, which will be released at 1130 GMT, will be one of the last high-profile platforms for the central bank to make known its views on monetary policy before the election.
Bank Governor Eddie George has been at odds with Chancellor Kenneth Clarke since December, when George's advice to raise interest rates to 6.25 percent from 6.0 percent was rejected.

"I think there will be a reiteration of the Bank's stance that the near-term outlook for inflation is perfectly OK but that, on a two-year view, policy needs to be tightened now to hit the 2.5 percent inflation target," says Paul Turnbull, an economist at Merrill Lynch.
In its last inflation report in November, the Bank said achievement of the inflation target remained elusive and a further rise in interest rates would be likely in due course.

Minutes of the December 11 monetary meeting show George warned that, if his call for an immediate quarter-point interest rate rise was not heeded, he would probably advise a half-point increase in January or February.
Clarke left rates unchanged at regular monetary meetings in both those months.
In an unusually forthright speech on January 20, George rejected Clarke's argument that the strength of sterling, which makes imports cheaper, was an important deflationary factor.
George said there could be real dangers in letting justified concern about the damaging effect of the strong pound on exports deflect attention from the need to tighten policy.
Richard Jeffrey, group economist at Charterhouse, expects the Bank to revise its inflation projections slightly higher in Wednesday's report.
"I think the warning that base rates have to rise will be much more explicit. We might find that the inflation forecasts for the second half of this year are pushed up quite a lot," he said.
Jeffrey also expects the Bank to develop its argument that sterling is not a key factor in the inflation outlook at the moment. "They will talk about inflation being demand-led," he said.

He will be interested to see if the Bank's comments on wages and earnings echo the view recently expressed by the U.S. Federal Reserve about the U.S. economy that the period of low wage inflation is coming to an end.
"If the Bank starts talking the same way we will get a good insight into they way they view cost pressures and things like that," Jeffrey said.
He shares the view of most economists that Clarke will leave interest rates unchanged until the election, due by May at the latest, "leaving the tough decisions to his successor."
John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International, says markets will be interested in how hawkish the Bank will be in the inflation report.

"I think the argument about higher rates has to do with an economy which is growing above trend and the pressures which may emerge as a consequence of that, perhaps at the retail level as retailers have some incentive to rebuild margins and as the output gap diminishes," he said.
Analysts at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell expect the Bank to warn that inflation is more likely than not to breach the 2.5 percent target in two years' time.
"We expect the Bank to be pushing for a 50 basis point rate rise, a request which is not likely to be met until after the election," they wrote in their weekly look-ahead.
